country.name: Mexico
country.tagline: The oldest winery in the Americas, a desert valley that became a culinary capital, and vineyards two kilometres up on the tropic's edge.

stats.note: ICEX España market study 2024: 39,956 ha of vineyard (all grape uses, including table grapes and brandy grapes), about 195,000 hl of wine, around 400 wineries, Baja California about 70 percent of wine production, Mexican wine about 34 percent of domestic consumption. Agricultura/SIAP: 83,178 t of wine grapes in 2025 (Baja California 30,934 t, Zacatecas 26,024 t, Aguascalientes 6,715 t) from 12 states.

country.overview:
Mexico is where wine in the Americas began. Spanish conquistadors needed wine for mass, and in 1524 Hernán Cortés ordered every Spaniard holding an encomienda to plant vines each year in proportion to the Indigenous people in his service. By the 1590s vines grew in the Parras valley of Coahuila, and Casa Madero, founded in 1597 as the Hacienda de San Lorenzo, is the oldest winery still operating in the Americas. Then Spain shut the door: Philip II banned new plantings in 1595 to protect Andalusian exporters, and later restrictions (a 1699 decree under Charles II is often cited) limited winemaking largely to the Church. Mexico's wine stayed a sacramental and frontier affair for three centuries while Peru, Chile and Argentina built industries.

Modern Mexican wine is concentrated in Baja California, where cold Pacific currents and a Mediterranean climate make the valleys behind Ensenada (Guadalupe, San Vicente, Santo Tomás, Ojos Negros) the source of most Mexican wine. Valle de Guadalupe grew from a handful of wineries in 1999 to about 150 by 2023 and became one of the country's great food destinations. In the central highlands, at 1,800 to 2,100 m in Querétaro, Guanajuato, Aguascalientes and Zacatecas, altitude offsets tropical latitude, though summer monsoon rains and hail make every vintage a gamble; Querétaro is known for sparkling wine. Parras in Coahuila, Chihuahua and Sonora complete the map.

The market is growing fast, with Mexican wine holding about a third of domestic consumption, but it is small: about 20 million litres a year and per capita consumption around 1.3 litres. In 2025 Querétaro obtained Mexico's first protected geographical indication for wine from IMPI, and Baja California producers launched their own IGP process in late 2025. Water is the existential issue in Baja, where vineyards depend on shrinking aquifers.

history.title: Cortés orders vines planted
history.text: Hernán Cortés decrees that Spaniards holding encomiendas must plant vines each year in proportion to the Indigenous people working for them (often summarised as 1,000 vines per 100 people).

history.title: Philip II bans new plantings
history.text: To protect Spanish wine exports, Philip II forbids new vineyards in the Americas; missions and churches are allowed to keep vines for sacramental wine. A later decree under Charles II (1699) is often cited as restricting winemaking to the Church.

history.title: Hacienda de San Lorenzo (Casa Madero)
history.text: Lorenzo García receives a land grant in the Parras valley and founds the Hacienda de San Lorenzo, today Casa Madero, the oldest winery in the Americas.

history.title: Mission vines in the Californias
history.text: Jesuit, then Dominican missionaries plant vines along Baja California; Santo Tomás (1791) and Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe del Norte (1834) are the ancestors of today's wine valleys.

history.title: Miguel Hidalgo's vines at Dolores
history.text: Father Miguel Hidalgo teaches his parishioners in Dolores to grow grapes, silk and pottery; colonial authorities order his vines destroyed. In 1810 he launches the War of Independence from the same parish.

history.title: Bodegas de Santo Tomás
history.text: Francisco Andonaegui and Miguel Ormart found Bodegas de Santo Tomás in Ensenada, Baja California's first commercial winery.

history.title: The Molokans arrive
history.text: About 100 families of Russian Molokans, pacifist Christian dissenters, settle the former mission lands of Valle de Guadalupe and plant wheat and vines.

history.title: Cetto in Tijuana
history.text: Angelo Cetto, an immigrant from Trentino, founds a winery in Tijuana; L.A. Cetto becomes Mexico's largest producer and plants the Valle de Guadalupe.

history.title: Monte Xanic
history.text: Hans Backhoff and partners found Monte Xanic in Valle de Guadalupe, the first boutique premium winery of modern Mexico.

history.title: Hugo D'Acosta and La Escuelita
history.text: Winemaker Hugo D'Acosta founds Casa de Piedra (1997) and later the Estación de Oficios del Porvenir ('La Escuelita'), a teaching winery that launches dozens of small labels.

history.title: First wine IGP
history.text: IMPI grants Mexico's first protected geographical indication for wine to the Querétaro wine region.

country.classification: Mexico has no national appellation system comparable to the AOC or AVA. Labels typically give the state and valley informally (Valle de Guadalupe, Valle de Parras). In 2025 the Instituto Mexicano de la Propiedad Industrial (IMPI) granted the first protected geographical indication (IGP) for wine, for the Querétaro wine region; Baja California's Comité Provino began an IGP process with El Colegio de la Frontera Norte in December 2025, and Coahuila producers are pursuing one. Wine policy is coordinated by the Consejo Mexicano Vitivinícola. Mexico imposes high excise taxes on wine, which weighs on prices.
country.climate_soils: Baja California's valleys are 20 to 40 km from the Pacific, with a Mediterranean climate, cool nights and marine breezes funnelled through canyons; soils are decomposed granite and sandy alluvium, and water comes from overdrawn aquifers. The central highlands rely on altitude (1,500 to 2,100 m) to offset latitude between 20 and 25 degrees north; the challenge is summer rain during ripening, hail and spring frost. Parras is a desert oasis fed by springs at about 1,500 m.

grapes.name: Nebbiolo
grapes.note: A Baja California speciality since the Cetto era, though much 'Nebbiolo' there has proved by DNA to be other varieties such as Lagrein.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: The most widely planted fine red; Casa Madero's Casa Grande and many Baja blends.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.note: Widespread in Baja and the highlands.

grapes.name: Grenache and Carignan
grapes.note: Old dry-farmed vines in Baja California.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.note: Historic white in Baja (Santo Tomás, L.A. Cetto).

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay
grapes.note: Main whites in Querétaro, Baja and Coahuila.

grapes.name: Mission (Misión)
grapes.note: The colonial grape, still found in old vineyards.

regions.name: Baja California
regions.tagline: Desert valleys behind Ensenada where Pacific fog, granite and Mediterranean grapes made Mexico's wine country.
regions.summary: Baja California produces most of Mexico's wine (about 70 percent by ICEX's estimate; some sources say up to 80 or 90 percent) from valleys strung along the inland side of the coastal hills north and south of Ensenada. Valle de Guadalupe is the heart, with about 150 wineries along the Ruta del Vino (Highway 3), plus restaurants that made it famous. San Antonio de las Minas, Valle de Santo Tomás, Valle de San Vicente, Ojos Negros, Valle de la Grulla and Tecate round out the region. Every August the Fiestas de la Vendimia celebrate harvest.
regions.history: Dominican missions (Santo Tomás 1791, Guadalupe del Norte 1834) planted the first vines. Bodegas de Santo Tomás was founded in 1888. Russian Molokans settled Valle de Guadalupe from 1905. L.A. Cetto (Tijuana 1928) and Casa Pedro Domecq (1972) industrialised the valley, then Monte Xanic (1987), Château Camou, Casa de Piedra (1997) and the graduates of Hugo D'Acosta's La Escuelita created a boutique movement.
regions.terroir: Mediterranean climate with cold Pacific influence; dry summers, little winter rain. Decomposed granite and sandy alluvial soils; salinity and falling aquifers are serious problems.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, Nebbiolo, Merlot, Syrah, Grenache, Carignan, Zinfandel, Chenin Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay.
regions.styles: Ripe, often blended reds with saline freshness; crisp whites from cooler Ojos Negros and San Vicente; rosé.
regions.classification: No legal appellations yet; Baja producers began an IGP process in December 2025.

regions.name: Coahuila
regions.tagline: A spring-fed oasis in the Chihuahuan Desert where the oldest winery in the Americas still makes wine.
regions.summary: Coahuila's Parras valley, at about 1,500 m, owes its name ('grapevines') to the wild vines Spanish explorers found around its springs. Casa Madero, founded as the Hacienda de San Lorenzo in 1597, is the oldest winery in the Americas still operating. The state also has vineyards in the Sierra de Arteaga near Saltillo, at higher elevations, and at Cuatro Ciénegas, where Bodegas Ferriño has made wine since the 19th century. Coahuila producers are pursuing a protected geographical indication.
regions.history: Spanish and Tlaxcalan settlers founded Santa María de las Parras in 1598. Evaristo Madero bought the San Lorenzo hacienda in the 1870s; his grandson Francisco I. Madero, born in Parras, led the 1910 Mexican Revolution and became president.
regions.terroir: High desert valley with springs and irrigation; hot days and cool nights; alluvial and limestone-derived soils.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Merlot, Tempranillo, Chardonnay, Chenin Blanc.
regions.styles: Structured reds and fresh whites; brandy.
regions.classification: No appellation; Coahuila is seeking an IG.

regions.name: Querétaro
regions.tagline: Sparkling wine and fresh whites at 2,000 m, holder of Mexico's first wine IGP.
regions.summary: Querétaro's vineyards lie on the high plateau around Ezequiel Montes, Tequisquiapan, Colón and Cadereyta, at about 1,800 to 2,100 m. Altitude makes days warm and nights cold, but summer rain and hail during ripening keep alcohol low and acidity high, ideal for sparkling wine and fresh whites and rosés. Freixenet de México (Sala Vivé) and La Redonda built the region in the 1970s and 1980s, and it now has more than 40 wine projects and the busiest wine tourism in central Mexico. In 2025 IMPI granted Querétaro Mexico's first protected geographical indication for wine.
regions.history: Grapes have appeared on Querétaro's coat of arms since 1655. Modern viticulture began in the 1960s and 1970s with brandy and sparkling-wine companies.
regions.terroir: High plateau with volcanic and calcareous soils; summer monsoon rain; frost and hail risk.
regions.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Macabeo, Xarel-lo, Pinot Noir, Malbec, Tempranillo, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot.
regions.styles: Traditional-method sparkling wine, fresh whites and rosés, light reds.
regions.classification: IGP for the Querétaro wine region (IMPI, 2025).

regions.name: Central Highlands (Bajío and Altiplano)
regions.tagline: Tropic-edge vineyards at altitude, from Hidalgo's Dolores to the brandy grapes of Zacatecas.
regions.summary: The Bajío and Altiplano states (Guanajuato, Aguascalientes, Zacatecas, San Luis Potosí) grow grapes between about 1,800 and 2,100 m, where altitude compensates for latitude. Zacatecas and Aguascalientes are large grape producers (26,024 t and 6,715 t of industrial grapes in 2025), much of it historically for brandy; Guanajuato around Dolores Hidalgo and San Miguel de Allende has become a fashionable wine-tourism destination.
regions.history: Miguel Hidalgo taught grape growing at Dolores before 1810; colonial authorities uprooted his vines. Aguascalientes' grape fair (Feria de la Uva) and brandy distilleries were 20th-century landmarks.
regions.terroir: High plateau; summer rain, hail and frost; volcanic and caliche soils.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Tempranillo, Malbec, Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc.

regions.name: Northern Mexico (Chihuahua and Sonora)
regions.tagline: Desert irrigation and Jesuit mission vines: brandy, table grapes and a new wine scene.
regions.summary: Sonora is Mexico's largest grape-growing state, but mostly for table grapes and brandy, around Hermosillo and Caborca. Chihuahua has wineries around Delicias, Encinillas and Casas Grandes at high elevation, and Jesuit mission vines survive at Cerocahui in the Copper Canyon.
regions.history: Jesuit missionaries planted vines at missions across the Sierra Madre in the 17th and 18th centuries.
regions.terroir: Hot deserts with irrigation; high plateaus in Chihuahua with cold winters.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Tempranillo, Chenin Blanc, table and brandy grapes.

mx-aguascalientes.name: Aguascalientes
mx-aguascalientes.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, Merlot, Chenin Blanc
mx-aguascalientes.summary: A central state at about 1,900 m with a long grape tradition: brandy houses and a famous grape harvest fair (Feria de la Uva) in the 20th century, and 6,715 t of industrial grapes in 2025. Modern wineries include Vinícola Santa Elena and Hacienda de Letras.

mx-chihuahua.name: Chihuahua
mx-chihuahua.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Tempranillo, Chenin Blanc
mx-chihuahua.summary: Northern state with wineries around Delicias, Encinillas and Casas Grandes at high elevation, and mission vines at Cerocahui in the Copper Canyon, planted by Jesuits.

mx-guanajuato.name: Guanajuato
mx-guanajuato.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Tempranillo, Malbec, Sauvignon Blanc
mx-guanajuato.summary: Guanajuato's vineyards lie around Dolores Hidalgo and San Miguel de Allende at about 1,900 to 2,100 m. Father Miguel Hidalgo taught his parishioners at Dolores to grow vines before the 1810 War of Independence, and the viceroyalty had them destroyed; the area's modern wine revival began in the 2000s with Cuna de Tierra and now includes estates around San Miguel such as Dos Búhos and San Lucas.

mx-queretaro.name: Querétaro
mx-queretaro.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Macabeo, Xarel-lo, Parellada, Pinot Noir, Malbec, Tempranillo, Cabernet Sauvignon
mx-queretaro.summary: Mexico's first protected geographical indication for wine, granted by IMPI and launched in April 2025, covering the wine region of Querétaro state. Vineyards sit around Ezequiel Montes, Tequisquiapan, Colón and Cadereyta at about 1,800 to 2,100 m, among the highest in North America. Days are warm, nights cold and summer rain coincides with ripening, so grapes keep high acidity and moderate sugar: ideal for traditional-method sparkling wine, which is the region's speciality. Freixenet de México at Ezequiel Montes, with deep underground cellars, has made traditional-method sparkling wine here since the 1980s; La Redonda, Viñedos Azteca, De Cote and Puerta del Lobo make still wines.

mx-san-antonio-de-las-minas.name: San Antonio de las Minas
mx-san-antonio-de-las-minas.summary: A small valley just south of Valle de Guadalupe, on the road to Ensenada, where Hugo D'Acosta founded Casa de Piedra in 1997 and the teaching winery La Escuelita. Slightly cooler and more exposed to marine air than Guadalupe.

mx-san-luis-potosi.name: San Luis Potosí
mx-san-luis-potosi.summary: A high-desert state on the Altiplano with a small but growing number of wineries, part of the central highland expansion, at about 1,800 to 2,000 m. Like its neighbours, it relies on altitude for cool nights and battles summer rain and hail.

mx-sierra-de-arteaga.name: Sierra de Arteaga
mx-sierra-de-arteaga.summary: A cooler, higher wine area (around 2,000 m) in the mountains east of Saltillo, near the town of Arteaga, with apple orchards and new boutique wineries.

mx-sonora.name: Sonora
mx-sonora.grapes: Table and brandy grapes, Cabernet Sauvignon
mx-sonora.summary: Mexico's largest grape-growing state, but mostly for export table grapes and for brandy, in irrigated desert around Hermosillo and Caborca. Wine production is small, though a few wineries have appeared, and the Jesuit missions of the Pimería Alta once grew vines here.

mx-valle-de-guadalupe.name: Valle de Guadalupe
mx-valle-de-guadalupe.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, Nebbiolo, Merlot, Syrah, Grenache, Zinfandel, Chenin Blanc
mx-valle-de-guadalupe.summary:
Mexico's most famous wine valley, about 20 km northeast of Ensenada along Highway 3, the Ruta del Vino. Dominicans founded the mission of Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe del Norte here in 1834; Russian Molokan families farmed the valley from 1905 (their museum survives in Francisco Zarco); L.A. Cetto and Domecq industrialised it from the 1970s; and Monte Xanic (1987), Château Camou, Adobe Guadalupe, Casa de Piedra and dozens of boutique wineries turned it into a food-and-wine destination, from 6 wineries in 1999 to about 150 in 2023.

The climate is Mediterranean, with hot days moderated by Pacific air drawn through the canyon from El Sauzal, and the soils are sandy decomposed granite. Reds dominate: Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, Nebbiolo, Merlot, Grenache and blends that combine ripe fruit with a saline, slightly bitter edge. Water is the valley's crisis: vineyards draw on an overexploited aquifer, and salinity is rising.

mx-valle-de-la-grulla.name: Valle de la Grulla
mx-valle-de-la-grulla.summary: A small valley on the road south of Ensenada around Ejido Uruapan and Santo Tomás, also called Valle de Uruapan, with old Grenache and Carignan vines and a cooler, coastal-influenced climate.

mx-valle-de-ojos-negros.name: Valle de Ojos Negros
mx-valle-de-ojos-negros.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir
mx-valle-de-ojos-negros.summary: A high inland valley east of Ensenada at about 700 m, cooler at night than the coastal valleys, with snow on the surrounding mountains in winter. Monte Xanic and others grow fresh Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay and Pinot Noir here.

mx-valle-de-parras.name: Valle de Parras
mx-valle-de-parras.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Merlot, Tempranillo, Chardonnay, Chenin Blanc
mx-valle-de-parras.summary: A spring-fed valley in the Chihuahuan Desert of southern Coahuila, at about 1,500 m, named for its wild vines. Casa Madero's Hacienda de San Lorenzo (1597) is the oldest winery in the Americas, and several family wineries and brandy distilleries surround the colonial town of Parras de la Fuente. Hot days, cold nights and spring water give structured Cabernet and Shiraz and crisp Chardonnay.
producers: Vinícola San Juan de la Vaquería

mx-valle-de-san-vicente.name: Valle de San Vicente
mx-valle-de-san-vicente.summary: A broad valley about 90 km south of Ensenada around San Vicente, with a Dominican mission founded in 1780. Warm and dry, it supplies grapes to many Guadalupe wineries and grows Cabernet, Tempranillo and Grenache.

mx-valle-de-santo-tomas.name: Valle de Santo Tomás
mx-valle-de-santo-tomas.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay
mx-valle-de-santo-tomas.summary: A valley about 45 km south of Ensenada, site of the Dominican mission of Santo Tomás de Aquino (1791) and the vineyards of Bodegas de Santo Tomás, Baja California's first commercial winery (1888). Cooler, windier and with heavier soils than Guadalupe.

mx-valle-de-tecate.name: Valle de Tecate
mx-valle-de-tecate.summary: The northernmost Baja wine area, around the border town of Tecate, at about 500 m. Rancho La Puerta's vineyards and small wineries grow Rhône and Bordeaux varieties.

mx-zacatecas.name: Zacatecas
mx-zacatecas.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, Merlot, Ruby Cabernet
mx-zacatecas.summary: A high-plateau state (about 2,000 m) that was Mexico's second-largest wine-grape producer in 2025 (26,024 t), mostly around Ojocaliente and Luis Moya, historically supplying brandy distillers. A handful of wineries now bottle Cabernet, Tempranillo and Merlot.

sites.name: Casa Madero (Hacienda de San Lorenzo)
sites.text: Founded in 1597 when Lorenzo García received a land grant in the Parras valley, the Hacienda de San Lorenzo is the oldest winery in the Americas still in operation. The Madero family bought it in the 1870s; Francisco I. Madero, leader of the 1910 Revolution, was born in nearby Parras. Its Casa Grande Cabernet and Shiraz are among Mexico's best-known wines.

sites.name: L.A. Cetto
sites.text: Angelo Cetto, from Trentino, began making wine in Tijuana in 1928; his son Luis Agustín founded L.A. Cetto in Valle de Guadalupe in the 1970s, and it became Mexico's largest wine producer, known for Nebbiolo and Petite Sirah.

sites.name: Monte Xanic
sites.text: Founded in 1987 by Hans Backhoff and partners as the first premium boutique winery of modern Mexico; its Gran Ricardo Bordeaux blend became a benchmark.

sites.name: Casa de Piedra
sites.text: Hugo D'Acosta's stone winery (1997), whose Vino de Piedra helped show that Baja could make serious red wine. D'Acosta's teaching winery, La Escuelita, launched dozens of small producers.

sites.name: Museo de la Vid y el Vino
sites.text: Baja California's state wine museum on the Ruta del Vino, in a modern building set among vineyards at the entrance to Valle de Guadalupe. Its exhibits trace vines from the Jesuit and Dominican missions through the Molokan settlers and the Cetto and Domecq era to the boutique wineries of today.

sites.name: Museo Comunitario del Valle de Guadalupe (Molokan museum)
sites.text: In the village of Francisco Zarco, a small museum in an old Russian Molokan house recalls the pacifist Christian families who settled the valley from 1905 and planted its first commercial vineyards and wheat fields.

sites.name: Bodegas de Santo Tomás
sites.text: Founded in Ensenada in 1888 by Francisco Andonaegui and Miguel Ormart on former mission lands of Santo Tomás de Aquino (1791), Baja California's first commercial winery. It now farms the Santo Tomás valley.

sites.name: Freixenet de México (Finca Sala Vivé)
sites.text: The Catalan cava house Freixenet chose Ezequiel Montes in the 1970s; its traditional-method sparkling wines age in deep underground cellars, and it anchors Querétaro's wine route.

sites.name: Viñedos La Redonda
sites.text: One of Querétaro's pioneering wineries, founded in the 1970s on the high plateau near Ezequiel Montes at about 1,900 m. Its still and sparkling wines and busy harvest festivals helped turn the Querétaro wine and cheese route into central Mexico's main wine-tourism destination.

sites.name: Cuna de Tierra
sites.text: A winery near Dolores Hidalgo whose vineyards helped revive wine in Hidalgo's town; its name ('cradle of earth') nods to Dolores as the cradle of Mexican independence.

sites.name: Parroquia de Dolores (Miguel Hidalgo)
sites.text: From this parish church Father Miguel Hidalgo issued the Grito de Dolores on 16 September 1810. As priest he had taught villagers to cultivate vines, mulberries for silk and pottery, industries the Spanish crown restricted; officials ordered his vines destroyed.

sites.name: Cerocahui mission
sites.text: A Jesuit mission founded in the late 17th century deep in the Copper Canyon where mission-era vines are still tended and a little wine is made, a reminder of the colonial vineyards that once dotted the Sierra Madre.
